title: 1 Samuel 23:19–29
context: The Ziphites offer to betray David to Saul, who blesses them and urges a careful search. Saul closes in at the wilderness of Maon, surrounding David on the other side of a mountain, until news of a Philistine raid turns him back. The place is named for the parting. Versification: English 23:29 is Hebrew 24:1; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: Then the Ziphites came up to Saul to Gibeah, saying, “Doesn’t David hide himself with us in the strongholds in the woods, in the hill of Hachilah, which is on the south of the desert?
verses.arminianNotes: The Ziphites go to Saul and reveal David’s hiding place. Arminian readers note the betrayal by people of David’s own tribe, a painful reminder that faithfulness can be met with treachery.
verses.reformedNotes: The superscription of Psalm 54 links that psalm to this betrayal. Reformed readers see David’s prayers in such moments as a model of trusting God when people turn against us.

verses.text: Now therefore, O king, come down. According to all the desire of your soul to come down; and our part will be to deliver him up into the king’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Ziphites urge Saul to come and promise to hand David over. Arminian readers see them choosing to side with power, a decision for which they are responsible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the eagerness of the offer: according to all the desire of your soul. The Ziphites cater to Saul’s obsession, showing how easily people serve a ruler’s sinful desires.

verses.text: Saul said, “You are blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul blesses the Ziphites in the LORD’s name for having compassion on him. Arminian readers notice the self-pity of a king who casts himself as the victim, and religious language used to cover a murderous aim he freely pursues.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the misuse of God’s name to bless betrayal. Saul’s piety has become a cover for hostility to God’s anointed, a sober warning that religious speech can coexist with resistance to God’s purposes.

verses.text: Please go make yet more sure, and know and see his place where his haunt is, and who has seen him there; for I have been told that he is very cunning.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks the Ziphites to make more sure of David’s haunts, calling him very cunning. Arminian readers note the contrast between Saul’s careful human planning and David’s dependence on God’s guidance through the ephod.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul’s calculations, however thorough, cannot overcome God’s purpose. The detailed instructions only set the stage for God’s intervention at Maon, where all of Saul’s preparation comes to nothing.

verses.text: See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hides himself; and come again to me with certainty, and I will go with you. It shall happen, if he is in the land, that I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul vows to search David out among all the thousands of Judah. Arminian readers see determination that has hardened into obsession, consuming the energy a king should spend protecting his people from the Philistines.
verses.reformedNotes: The sweeping vow fails within a few verses. Reformed readers see a reminder that no human search can find someone God chooses to hide, a theme Psalm 54, linked by its heading to the Ziphites, takes up in prayer.

verses.text: They arose, and went to Ziph before Saul; but David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah on the south of the desert.
verses.arminianNotes: The Ziphites go ahead of Saul, but David has already moved to the wilderness of Maon. Arminian readers note David’s practical caution as part of a faithful response to danger, not a substitute for trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the movements of both parties under God’s governance. David stays a step ahead, not by luck, but within the providence that 23:14 has already announced.

verses.text: Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told, he went down to the rock, and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard that, he pursued David in the wilderness of Maon.
verses.arminianNotes: David goes down to the rock in the wilderness of Maon, and Saul follows. Arminian readers feel the pressure tightening as the chase narrows, a test of whether David will keep trusting when escape routes close.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the narrator builds suspense: each move by David is matched by Saul. The account prepares readers to see that rescue, when it comes, cannot be credited to David’s skill.

verses.text: Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain; and David hurried to get away for fear of Saul, for Saul and his men surrounded David and his men to take them.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul and David are on opposite sides of the mountain, and Saul’s men are surrounding David. Arminian readers see a moment of real peril in which David’s own efforts are no longer enough to save him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as a picture of extremity, the point at which only God can deliver. A single mountain is all that stands between the anointed and the king who hunts him.

verses.text: But a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid on the land!”
verses.arminianNotes: A messenger arrives: the Philistines have raided the land. Arminian readers see God’s providential care in the timing, working through events and the choices of others to rescue David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign hand in the Philistine raid, an event outside David’s control that turns Saul back at the decisive moment. Both traditions see providence here.

verses.text: So Saul returned from pursuing David, and went against the Philistines. Therefore they called that place Sela Hammahlekoth.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul turns back to fight the Philistines, and the place is named Sela Hammahlekoth. The meaning is usually given as rock of parting. Arminian readers see the name as a memorial to God’s deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same Philistines David fought at Keilah now become, unknowingly, the means of his rescue. The name preserves the memory of how close the danger came.

verses.text: David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En Gedi.
verses.arminianNotes: David moves up to the strongholds of En Gedi, an oasis near the Dead Sea. Arminian readers note that after a narrow escape he continues to take sensible precautions, combining trust in God with wise action.
verses.reformedNotes: This verse is 24:1 in the Hebrew text, which links the escape directly to the next scene; the WEB numbering is kept here. Reformed readers see David’s new refuge setting up the encounter in the cave.
